claim: Fixation (failing to revise an assessment while cues against it accumulate) is common in human crisis handling, in two simulator studies with different units. Schwid and O'Donnell (1992): fixation errors or failure to revise in 63% of 30 anesthesiologists (10 residents, 10 faculty, 10 private practice). DeAnda and Gaba (1990): fixation was 20.5% of 132 unplanned incidents (27 incidents) over 19 resident simulations. Not comparable as rates. No replication that reuses the 63% scoring was found. Woods and Cook define fixation by two tests: persistence over time and revision cues that were available. In 2026 LLM SRE agents the same pattern is described in case studies (SREGym), with no prevalence.
agent_test: Replay a fixed set of fault scripts (wrong first hypothesis, contradicting evidence arrives at step 3 to 6) and count the share of runs where the agent keeps the first hypothesis for 3 or more further steps; compare scaffold with and without the detector at equal tokens.

claim: An LLM given information piecemeal commits early and does not recover: 15 models lost 39% on average from single-turn to multi-turn, mostly through unreliability (+112%) rather than aptitude (-15%). Anchoring work points the same way but is weak.
agent_test: Stage the same task as full prompt versus evidence revealed in 4 shards; measure the drop with and without a code-held fact record and a restart from a clean summary.

claim: Asking a model to re-check its own answer without external information does not help and often hurts (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after 2 rounds; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1). With oracle labels it helps (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5; HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0; GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3). A survey agrees: no success from prompted-LLM feedback outside special tasks.
agent_test: Compare revise-on-schedule, revise-on-model-doubt and revise-on-code-failure at equal tokens on tasks with a checkable output.

claim: Locating the error is the weak step for LLMs; repairing it once located is the strong step. Mistake-finding in chain-of-thought traces: 52.87% best (GPT-4); failure attribution: 53.5% agent, 14.2% step; TRAIL best joint 18.3% on GAIA split and 5.0% on SWE split. Backtracking from the true location gains 18 to 44 points on originally wrong answers.
agent_test: Give the repair step either the code-found failing step (first failed test, diff, counter) or a model-found step; measure repair success at equal tokens.

claim: LLM agents repeat the same failing action until the budget ends. AIOpsLab: same malformed call up to 14 times in a 20-step case (GPT-3.5); MAST: step repetition 15.7% of failure labels; AgentBench: Task Limit Exceeded is the commonest outcome on several tasks; Reflexion uses a repeat-more-than-3-cycles or 30-action rule as its trigger. BOUNDARY (2026): on Cloud-OpsBench, strong models (GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Flash) have a Redundant Action Rate near 0.00; only weak models loop (Qwen3-8B 0.46, Qwen3-14B 0.28). For small models the failed call text in context raises the repeat chance (6 models, 135M to 1.7B).
agent_test: Detector rule: identical action plus identical error N times, or a step cap with no new evidence. Log how often it fires and what share of fires were true stalls. Run on a weak and a strong model: the repeat rule is expected to fire mostly on the weak one.

claim: More steps stop helping early on operations tasks. GPT-3.5 gained nothing past 5 steps; FLASH reached its best 59.32% only at step limit 20. The authors say self-repair from environment feedback saturates quickly. Only one paper, four agents.
agent_test: Sweep step cap (5, 10, 20) with and without a strategy switch at the stall point at equal total tokens.

claim: There is a large drop from detection to fixing. AIOpsLab (48 problems, re-checked): detection FLASH 100%, ReAct 76.92%, GPT-4 69.23%; RCA 36.36 to 45.45% for the top three; mitigation FLASH 54.55%, ReAct 36.36%, GPT-4 27.27%, GPT-3.5 0%. ITBench SRE: best 13.8% resolved, GPT-4o diagnosis 13.81% pass@1, mitigation 11.43%. 2026 frontier models still fall short: ITBench-AA best 47% (Claude Opus 4.7) and 46% (GPT-5.5); SREGym mitigation 40.4% to 78.5%, end-to-end best 60.7%, and end-to-end on new failure types 15.4% to 28.2%; Cloud-OpsBench best JRA 0.76 but evidence closure 0.38. The gap between a right answer and its supporting evidence persists.
agent_test: Score our agent per phase (notice, locate, explain, act) on injected faults, not only final answer.

claim: Success falls with difficulty and with less observability. ITBench GPT-4o diagnosis 36%, 7.73%, 5.0% for easy, medium, hard; mitigation 21%, 12.27%, 0.0%; without traces diagnosis 13.81% to 9.52%. The paper's own appendix gives 18.10% with traces, which conflicts with the main text.
agent_test: Mask one signal source in a fault task and measure whether the agent asks for it (epistemic move) or guesses.

claim: Tool-grounded investigation cuts invented causes but does not raise accuracy. Roy et al. (97 labelled cases, re-checked): correct 35% ReAct vs 39% CoT and retrieval; hallucination 4% vs 12% and 40%; 66% of ReAct's wrong answers are give-ups against 32% CoT and 18% retrieval.
agent_test: Compare give-up rate and wrong-confident rate with and without a tool-evidence step; check the give-up path hands off to a revise step.

claim: Structure around the model raises stability more than prompting. RCAgent (re-checked): pass within 15 steps 99.38% vs ReAct 86.33%, invalid actions 7.93% vs 22.82%; swapping in SQL tools gave 65.84% pass and 70.94% invalid; SWE-agent linting guard 18.0% vs 15.0% (wide error bars, not re-checked).
agent_test: Add a code-side action validator (format, known tool, no exact repeat) and compare invalid-action rate at equal tokens.

claim: External checklists or cognitive aids cut omitted critical steps in human crises: surgical-ward teams 33% to 10% (25 teams per arm, 75 scenarios per arm; Koers et al. 2020); operating-room crises 23% to 6% missed steps (17 teams, 106 scenarios; Arriaga et al. 2013). Both re-checked; both measure omissions, not fixation.
agent_test: Code-held list of required checks before an answer is accepted; compare omitted-check rate with and without it.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Verification gaps are a large share of multi-agent failures (MAST: task verification group 21.3%; no or incomplete verification 8.2%, incorrect verification 9.1%), and adding a task-objective verification step gave +15.6% on ProgramDev. One framework tested.
agent_test: Add a code-run verification of the final answer against the stated objective and measure the change.

claim: Automation bias (accepting an automated hint without checking) is found in experts, rises with workload, complexity and time pressure, and is not removed by training or instructions. Showing information rather than a recommendation reduced it. Evidence is abstract-level only.
agent_test: Present tool evidence without a proposed answer and measure how often a planted wrong hint is accepted.

claim: HUMAN: a person with a fresh point of view usually breaks a fixation (Woods and Cook, summarising Woods et al. 1987 incident data; now read directly, no rates). LLM: a fresh rollout with no history adds almost nothing on its own. FailFast-RestartSmart (SWE-bench Verified, 3 open models): cold restart +0.2 to +2.6 points, and it threw away 27.5% to 36.4% of runs that would have passed on Qwen3.6-27B; fresh start plus the old run's code diff gave +3.0 to +5.2 and lost 8.8% to 15.2%. For 0.5B models under greedy decoding, clearing the failed step raised the repeat rate from 31% to 80%. The old clear-the-context advice (Yang 2026, unverified) is therefore incomplete: what is carried across matters. Outside feedback still beats same-context reflection in the Huang line (K03).
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens: same-context reflection; clean restart with the evidence list only; clean restart with evidence list plus verified partial results. Count stuck-then-recovered runs and wrongly-aborted runs.

claim: Switching attention on every signal (thematic vagabonding, Dorner 1983 via Woods and Cook) is the opposite failure to fixation, and revising has a cost. No measured best switching rate exists for humans or LLMs. Closest LLM data: fixed-interval checks every 3, 5 or 7 steps lose to event-driven checks (OSWorld 55.1% at $0.07 vs 58.2% at $0.05; WebArena 52.5% vs 58.8%), and a false-positive-budget sweep of 5% to 25% shows recall rising 30.5% to 68.3% while precision falls 76.1% to 58.8% (Qwen3.6-27B). On Qwen3.5-9B the best resolve gain came at 10% FPR (+4.0) and 25% added none (+3.8).
agent_test: Sweep doubt trigger frequency (never, on signal, every N steps, event-driven with a false-alarm budget of 5, 10, 25%); measure accuracy and wrongly-aborted runs at equal tokens.

claim: Raw or irrelevant data in context harms the reasoning. AIOpsLab: failed cases leaned on raw metric/trace calls and dumped telemetry; GSM-IC: one irrelevant sentence cuts accuracy sharply; Lost in the middle: drops over 20% when the answer sits mid-context.
agent_test: Summarise tool output in code to a fixed-size record before the model sees it; compare to raw dumps at equal tokens. Existing 2026 evidence is confounded: Stratus (preprocesses data) used 1.81x fewer tokens than Claude Code with the same model but diagnosed less often (61.5% vs 72.6%).

claim: Alarm and signal design: useful signals are context-sensitive, partial and non-interrupting; nuisance alarms and status flooding fail. Evidence is case-based and read only through a blog summary.
agent_test: Detector emits a short reason code, not a full interruption; compare to a verbose alert.

claim: Garden-path problems: early cues point to a plausible wrong answer and later weaker cues to the right one. Conceptual argument, not measured.
agent_test: Build items where early evidence misleads; test whether late weak contradicting evidence is re-weighed.

claim: A single co-occurring improvement can confirm a wrong model (Kegworth: throttling the wrong engine stopped vibration; about 20 minutes of wrong diagnosis). Case study from a secondary summary.
agent_test: Plant a wrong fix that makes the visible output look better; check whether a test against the original failing output catches it.

claim: Detection needs a baseline of normal: in AIOpsLab's no-fault problems only GPT-4 said normal and the others raised false alarms (not re-checked; the paper confirms this only through the extract). Model-judged triggers also err both ways: in Ambig-SWE the 'is this underspecified' judgment has false-positive and false-negative rates from 0.00 to 1.00 depending on model and prompt (Sonnet 4 default 0.08 and 0.44; Qwen 3 Coder 0.00 and 1.00; Llama 3.1 70B 0.95 and 0.09).
agent_test: Include no-fault items and measure false-alarm rate of the detector. Report separately for a code rule and for a model-judged rule.

claim: Targeted feedback from a located root-cause step improves agents, but the locator is weak. AgentDebug (GPT-4.1 with a structured taxonomy prompt): step accuracy 45.0% vs 28.0% for direct prompting, all-correct (step, module and type) 24.3% vs 0.3%; kappa 0.55 on 200 trajectories; re-rolling out from the found step lifted ALFWorld success (GPT-4o-mini 21 to 55, Qwen3-8B 48 to 74, Qwen3-Next-80B 60 to 84). Authors' own benchmark, no independent replication found. The tension with K04 is plausibly length: Who&When shows attribution accuracy falling with log length (5 to 130 steps) to near 0% at the longest, and random guessing scores 19.06% step-level on its short algorithm-made logs. No source tests this directly.
agent_test: Replace the LLM locator with a code locator and compare. Also bin runs by length and report locator accuracy per bin.

claim: Role or teamwork prompt changes do not fix inter-agent misalignment (MAST: +9.4% from clearer role specs on ChatDev; verification failures remain). Single framework.
agent_test: Not needed for a single-agent design; keep as a reason not to add personas.

claim: A learned stuck or failure monitor with an escalation or restart action raises success at the same or lower cost than no monitor or a fixed-interval check. Stuck Monitor on OSWorld and WebArena: small model alone 43.3% and 30.3%, with monitors and a stronger model 58.2% and 58.8%; held-out stuck-detector accuracy 93.9%. FailFast on SWE-bench Verified: Qwen3.6-27B resolve 66.6% to 71.8% with an alarm at 25% FPR and restart with diff overlay. Caveats: in the first study the gain mixes detection with a stronger model taking over; in the second, one benchmark and open models only.
agent_test: Impasse detector on/off at equal tokens on injected-fault runs, with the same model doing the recovery.

claim: A code-run step-count rule is a strong low-cost baseline for impasse detection, but a learned monitor is better. In FailFast (Qwen3.6-27B, 5% FPR) the step-count-only control caught 19.8% of failing runs against 30.5% for the learned monitor and 21.0% for AgentStop; at 25% FPR 50.9% vs 68.3%. On Qwen3.5-9B at 5% FPR all three tie (34.7, 35.1, 34.7). No study tests a repeat-action or no-new-evidence counter, or compares a code counter with a model-judged 'am I stuck' at equal tokens (gap 1 stays open).
agent_test: Arms at equal tokens: no detector; step cap; repeat-plus-no-new-evidence counter in code; model-judged stuck flag. Report recall and false-alarm rate on fault scripts.

claim: False alarms cost real runs, and a carried-over state cuts the cost. FailFast: with cold restart 36.4% (10% FPR) and 27.5% (25%) of runs that would have passed were lost on Qwen3.6-27B; with the diff overlay 15.2% and 8.8%. A prompt-level intervention (SWE-PRM) gave +4.2 on a 9B model and -3.2 on the 27B. A detector's calibration can also shift when the agent changes (audit of early-outcome predictors: two of many agent pairs persistently off by 0.11 to 0.14; abstract only).
agent_test: Count would-have-succeeded runs the detector interrupted; recalibrate the threshold per model.

claim: Frontier 2025-2026 models were tested on newer fault benchmarks and still show the same shape. SREGym (live, 90 problems): diagnosis 38.1% to 72.6%, noise lowers diagnosis for every pair (e.g. Claude Code + Sonnet-4.6 72.6% to 62.6%), new failure types cut end-to-end success to 15.4% to 28.2%. ITBench-AA: Claude Opus 4.7 47%, GPT-5.5 46%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 30% with 83 turns vs 31 turns for GPT-5.5. Cloud-OpsBench: Joint RCA Accuracy up to 0.76 but Evidence Closure Rate 0.15 to 0.46 for the top models. AIOpsLab itself was not re-run on reasoning models in any source found (gap 5 partly closed).
agent_test: Use SREGym-style noise injection and Cloud-OpsBench-style evidence-closure scoring in the test set.

claim: Current LLM agents anchor on the first plausible anomaly and use it as the stopping rule. SREGym: all evaluated agents treat the first plausible anomaly as the target, even when it is injected noise; in one problem neither agent ever inspected the faulty component; in another the agent named the true cause as a candidate and kept the wrong one. Cloud-OpsBench: agents anchor on the loudest downstream symptom and treat an empty result as no evidence. Qualitative and author-selected in both; no prevalence.
agent_test: Add noise-anomaly scripts; measure the share of runs that ever inspect the true faulty component and that list a rival hypothesis.

claim: A wrong first diagnosis is often recovered by acting and watching whether the symptom persists. SREGym: P(mitigation | correct diagnosis) 68% to 89% vs 22% to 62% with a wrong diagnosis; with wrong diagnosis Stratus + Sonnet-4.6 made 3.82 mitigation attempts vs 1.88 with a right one.
agent_test: Trigger a revise step when the same symptom persists after an action, and count recoveries.

claim: A model-judged 'should I stop and ask' trigger is unreliable, and asking recovers a lot when it fires. Ambig-SWE: interaction gives up to 74% relative gain; Sonnet 4 reaches 89% of full-spec performance; detection false-positive and false-negative rates range from 0.00 to 1.00 across models and prompts. A scaffold that separates the check from the coder reports 69.40% vs 61.20% (abstract only).
agent_test: Trigger the ask from a code stall counter; let the model only write the question; compare with a model-judged trigger.

claim: The three Woods failure patterns (decompensation, working at cross-purposes, getting stuck in outdated behaviors) are a conceptual summary of adaptive-system failure (Woods and Branlat, 2011 chapter), not measured categories from the fault-management studies. No rates exist in any accessible source. NUREG/CR-6208 (Roth, Mumaw, Lewis 1994) could not be opened. The only measured pattern with a stated definition is fixation (persistence plus available revision cues). Map detector rules by mechanism, not by cited rate.
agent_test: Write one detector rule per mechanism and test each on its own injected fault script.
